course: Daily Milk Sales: Dairy Herd System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Calf rearing is the foundation of your dairy herd. A healthy calf today becomes a high-milk cow tomorrow. In Africa, many farmers lose calves to preventable diseases like scours (diarrhoea) and pneumonia. Each calf lost is a loss of future income. If you raise 10 calves successfully, you could have 10 new milking cows in two years, doubling your daily milk sales. Good calf rearing also means better growth: a well-fed calf can weigh 70-80 kg at 3 months and 200 kg at 6 months. That means earlier first calving at 24-30 months instead of 36-40 months, saving you feed costs and bringing milk sooner. In this module, you will learn practical steps to rear calves with limited resources. We focus on the first 12 weeks, the most critical period. You will learn how to feed colostrum, manage milk feeding, provide clean water and starter feed, and keep housing dry and clean. We also cover common mistakes like overfeeding milk or using dirty buckets. By the end, you will be able to set up a simple calf pen using local materials like poles, thatch, and wire mesh. You will also know how to spot sickness early and treat it. Remember, each calf you raise well is money in your pocket. Let's get started.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To rear calves successfully, you need basic tools and materials. Most can be found locally or made by a village carpenter. First, a calf pen: build a dry, well-ventilated shelter. Use wooden poles for posts (2-3 meters tall), thatch or iron sheets for roofing, and wire mesh or wooden slats for walls. The floor should be slightly sloped for drainage, covered with dry bedding like straw or wood shavings. Each calf needs at least 2 square meters of space. Second, feeding equipment: a clean plastic bucket (10-20 litres) for milk, a smaller bucket (5 litres) for water, and a calf bottle with a teat for young calves. You can also use a nipple bucket. Third, for feeding: fresh cow colostrum (first milk) within 2 hours of birth, then whole milk or milk replacer. If using milk replacer, mix 125g powder per litre of warm water (40Â°C). Fourth, for health: a thermometer, iodine for navel dipping, and a first-aid kit with antibiotics (consult vet), electrolytes for scours, and dewormer. Fifth, for record keeping: a notebook and pen to record birth date, feeding amounts, and health events. Sixth, for cleaning: a stiff brush, soap, and disinfectant. Also, have a calf jacket or old blanket for cold nights. Finally, a simple scale or weigh tape to monitor growth. All these items cost less than $100 and will save you many times that in calf survival.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps for successful calf rearing from birth to 12 weeks. Step 1: Immediately after birth, ensure the calf breathes. Clear mucus from nose and mouth. Dip navel in iodine to prevent infection. Step 2: Feed colostrum within 2 hours. Give 2 litres for a small calf, 3 litres for a large one. Colostrum is thick and yellow; if the dam cannot suckle, milk her by hand and feed the calf with a clean bottle. Feed colostrum for the first 3 days, 10% of body weight daily (e.g., 3 litres for a 30 kg calf). Step 3: From day 4 to week 2, feed whole milk at 10% of body weight per day, split into 2-3 feeds. For a 35 kg calf, that's 3.5 litres daily. Always feed at body temperature (38Â°C). Step 4: From week 3, introduce calf starter (dry feed) and fresh clean water. Offer a handful of starter after each milk feed. Increase gradually to 1 kg per day by week 8. Step 5: From week 5, reduce milk slowly. By week 8, feed only 1-2 litres per day. By week 12, wean completely if the calf eats 1.5 kg starter daily. Step 6: Provide hay or fresh grass from week 2. Step 7: Keep the pen clean: remove wet bedding daily, disinfect weekly. Step 8: Watch for sickness: scours (loose dung), pneumonia (coughing), or dullness. Treat scours with electrolytes and consult a vet. Step 9: Record everything: birth weight, daily milk, starter intake, and health events. Step 10: Weigh monthly to check growth. A healthy calf should gain 400-600g per day. If not, adjust feeding.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Many farmers lose calves due to avoidable mistakes. Here are common ones and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Not feeding colostrum soon enough. Colostrum must be given within 2 hours; after 6 hours, the calf cannot absorb antibodies. Fix: Always have a clean bottle ready and milk the dam immediately after birth. Mistake 2: Overfeeding milk. Giving too much milk causes scours. Fix: Stick to 10% of body weight per day, split into 2-3 feeds. For a 40 kg calf, that's 4 litres total, not 6. Mistake 3: Using dirty buckets. Bacteria cause scours. Fix: Wash buckets with hot water and soap after each feed, then rinse with disinfectant. Mistake 4: Feeding cold milk. Cold milk shocks the calf's stomach. Fix: Warm milk to 38Â°C (test with your wrist; it should feel neither hot nor cold). Mistake 5: Poor housing. Damp, drafty pens cause pneumonia. Fix: Keep bedding dry, ensure ventilation but no direct draft. Mistake 6: Weaning too early. Calves weaned before 8 weeks often stunt. Fix: Wean at 8-12 weeks only when eating 1.5 kg starter daily. Mistake 7: Ignoring sickness. Early signs like loose dung or coughing need quick action. Fix: Check calves daily; treat scours with electrolytes and call vet for pneumonia. Mistake 8: Not recording. Without records, you cannot spot problems. Fix: Keep a simple notebook. Mistake 9: Mixing calves of different ages. Older calves bully younger ones and spread disease. Fix: Group calves by age in separate pens. Mistake 10: Using antibiotics without vet advice. This leads to resistance. Fix: Consult a vet before treating. By avoiding these mistakes, you can achieve over 90% calf survival.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Calf rearing involves safety for both you and the calf. Follow these best practices. Personal safety: Always wash your hands with soap after handling calves, especially before eating. Wear boots and gloves when cleaning pens to avoid infections like leptospirosis. When lifting a calf, bend your knees, not your back. Calf safety: Handle calves gently. Never shout or hit them; this causes stress and poor growth. When moving a calf, use a halter or guide it with your arm around its chest. Ensure the pen has no sharp edges or wires that can cut. Best practices for health: Vaccinate calves according to vet advice (e.g., for anthrax, blackleg). Deworm at 4 and 8 weeks. Keep a footbath at the pen entrance to prevent disease spread. For feeding: Use clean, warm water for mixing milk replacer. Never feed spoiled milk or milk from a cow treated with antibiotics (withdrawal period). For housing: Ensure good drainage to prevent muddy, wet floors. Provide shade in hot weather and windbreaks in cold. For records: Record all treatments, vaccinations, and feed changes. For emergencies: Have a vet's phone number. If a calf has severe scours, isolate it and give electrolytes. If pneumonia, call vet immediately. For biosecurity: Limit visitors to the calf pen. Do not bring in new calves without quarantine. For environmental safety: Dispose of dead calves properly (deep burial or incineration) to prevent disease spread. By following these practices, you protect your investment and your health.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now put your knowledge into action with this practical exercise. You will rear a calf from birth to 12 weeks, recording all steps. If you don't have a calf, work with a neighbour or practice with a model. Step 1: Prepare a calf pen. Use local materials: poles, thatch, wire mesh. Ensure it is dry, clean, and has 2 square meters per calf. Step 2: Gather tools: bucket, bottle, thermometer, iodine, notebook. Step 3: At birth, dip navel in iodine, weigh the calf (use a scale or weigh tape). Record birth weight and date. Step 4: Feed 2-3 litres of colostrum within 2 hours. Record time and amount. Step 5: For the first 3 days, feed colostrum 3 times daily. Then switch to whole milk at 10% body weight. For a 35 kg calf, feed 3.5 litres daily, split into 2 feeds. Step 6: From week 1, offer clean water and a handful of starter after each milk feed. Increase starter gradually. Step 7: Weigh the calf weekly and record. Calculate average daily gain. Target: 400-600g per day. Step 8: Observe health daily. Check for scours, coughing, or dullness. If scours, give electrolytes. If not better in 24 hours, call vet. Step 9: At week 8, if calf eats 1.5 kg starter daily, reduce milk to 1 litre per day. At week 12, stop milk completely. Step 10: At week 12, weigh again. A healthy calf should weigh 70-90 kg. Write a one-page report: what went well, what challenges, and what you would change. Share with your group. This exercise builds real skills for your dairy business.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Calf Rearing for Profitable Daily Milk Sales

Calf rearing is the single most important investment a dairy enterprise makes in its future. Every litre of milk sold today funds the replacement heifer that will produce tomorrow. In East and Southern Africa, where smallholder dairy systems supply over 80% of marketed milk, calf mortality rates on farms without structured rearing programmes commonly reach 20â30%. Each lost calf represents not just an animal, but two to three years of lost future income, plus the sunk cost of the dam's gestation and lactation. This practical reference consolidates the tools, methods, benchmarks, and safety practices needed to rear calves successfully under African smallholder and emerging commercial conditions.

Tools and Materials Reference

Table 1: Essential Calf Rearing Tools and Their Function
Tool / Material Function Quantity (per calf) Local Sourcing
Calf bottle with teatControlled colostrum and milk feeding1Agrovet shops, KARI/NaLIRRI centres
Bucket (10â15 L)Milk and water delivery2Local hardware, supermarkets
Starter feed troughConcentrate feeding from week 11Fabricated locally or purchased
Hay rack / roughage feederForage delivery, reduces waste1Carpentry workshops
Calf pen / hutchIndividual housing, disease control1Local timber, off-cuts, poles
Bedding (dry straw/sawdust)Insulation, hygiene, comfort2â3 bales/weekFarm by-product or local market
Disinfectant (e.g., glutaraldehyde)Pen and equipment sanitation1 L/monthAgrovet shops
Thermometer & weigh tapeHealth monitoring, growth tracking1 eachVeterinary supply stores
Colostrum (frozen or fresh)Immune protection in first 2 hours2â3 LFrom dam or neighbour's dam
Calf starter pelletsRumen development, early weaning25â30 kg totalFeed manufacturers (e.g., Unga, Pembe)

Source: Compiled from FAO (2019), Dairy Production and Processing: A Practical Guide for Smallholders, and ILRI (2020) smallholder dairy extension materials.

Performance Benchmarks and Cost Analysis

Table 2: Calf Rearing Performance Benchmarks and Economic Impact (Kenya/Tanzania context)
Parameter Poor Practice Good Practice Economic Impact
Colostrum within 2 hrs< 50% of calves> 95% of calvesReduces mortality by 15â20%
Pre-weaning mortality20â30%< 5%Saves KES 45,000â70,000 per calf reared
Weaning age16â20 weeks10â12 weeksSaves 400â600 L of milk per calf
Daily live weight gain150â250 g/day400â500 g/dayHeifer calves reach puberty 4â6 months earlier
First calving age30â36 months24â27 monthsSaves KES 30,000â50,000 in rearing costs
Milk yield (first lactation)8â12 L/day15â20 L/dayAdditional KES 180,000â250,000 per lactation
Starter feed consumed5â10 kg25â30 kgCost: KES 1,200â1,800, ROI: 10â15x

Source: Adapted from Kenya Dairy Board (2021) Dairy Value Chain Performance Report and ILRI (2020) Smallholder Dairy Development in East Africa. Currency values are indicative and vary with market conditions.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Colostrum and Disease Control

Colostrum must be collected from a healthy dam with no signs of mastitis, Johnes disease, or brucellosis. Always use clean, disinfected containers. If using pooled colostrum, only pool from dams of the same herd with known health status. Never feed colostrum from a dam with a retained placenta or fever. Brucellosis and tuberculosis can be transmitted through raw colostrum and milk â pasteurise if disease status is unknown. Always wash hands and equipment with soap and clean water before and after handling calves. Wear protective gloves when assisting with difficult births. In case of scours (diarrhoea), isolate the calf immediately and consult a veterinarian â do not share feeding equipment between sick and healthy calves.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Colostrum within 2 hours: Feed 10% of body weight (3â4 L for a 35 kg calf) within the first 2 hours of birth, and another 10% within 6â8 hours.
  2. Clean, dry, draught-free housing: Individual calf pens or hutches with dry bedding changed daily. Minimum 1.5 mÂ² per calf.
  3. Consistent milk feeding: 10% of body weight per day, split into 2 feeds, at body temperature (38Â°C). Use a nipple bottle for first 2 weeks.
  4. Fresh water always available: Calves need water from day 1 for rumen development. Change at least twice daily.
  5. Starter feed from week 1: Offer small handfuls of high-quality calf starter daily. Target 1 kg/day by week 10 before weaning.
  6. Weigh and record weekly: Use a weigh tape or scale. Target 400â500 g/day gain. Record all weights in a calf register.
  7. Health monitoring: Check eyes, ears, nose, faeces, and navel daily. Treat scours and pneumonia immediately.
  8. Disinfect equipment and pens: Between calves, and weekly during rearing. Use approved disinfectants and allow to dry.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Dairy Production and Processing: A Practical Guide for Smallholders (free full PDF)
  • ILRI â Smallholder Dairy Development Publications (free extension materials)
  • Kenya Dairy Board â Farmer Resources and Guidelines (free registration)
  • CGIAR â Livestock and Dairy Research Briefs (open access)
  • USDA National Agricultural Library â Dairy Cattle Health and Management (free access)

Business note: Every KES 1,500 invested in proper calf rearing (colostrum, starter feed, housing) returns an estimated KES 15,000â22,000 in additional first-lactation milk revenue. Calf rearing is not a cost centre â it is the highest-ROI activity on a dairy farm. Track your calf performance monthly against the benchmarks in Table 2 and adjust management immediately when targets are missed.

quiz.q: Why is colostrum important for a newborn calf?
options: A) It provides antibodies for immunity
B) It is cheaper than milk
C) It helps the calf sleep
D) It makes the calf grow faster
quiz.explanation: Colostrum contains antibodies that protect the calf from diseases until its own immune system develops.

quiz.q: How soon after birth should a calf receive colostrum?
quiz.explanation: The calf can only absorb antibodies efficiently within the first 2 hours after birth.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily milk feeding amount for a calf?
quiz.explanation: Feeding 10% of body weight per day provides adequate nutrition without causing digestive upset.

quiz.q: At what temperature should milk be fed to a calf?
quiz.explanation: Milk at body temperature (38Â°C) is best for digestion and prevents cold shock.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of scours in calves?
quiz.explanation: Dirty buckets and bottles introduce bacteria that cause diarrhoea (scours).

quiz.q: When can a calf be weaned?
quiz.explanation: Calves should be weaned at 8-12 weeks when they are eating at least 1.5 kg of starter feed daily.

quiz.q: What is the minimum space required per calf in a pen?
quiz.explanation: Each calf needs at least 2 square meters to move freely and stay clean.

quiz.q: Which material is best for bedding in a calf pen?
quiz.explanation: Dry straw absorbs moisture and provides a clean, comfortable surface.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after a calf is born?
quiz.explanation: Dipping the navel in iodine prevents infection, which can be fatal.

quiz.q: What is a sign of pneumonia in a calf?
quiz.explanation: Coughing, along with rapid breathing and fever, is a common sign of pneumonia.

quiz.q: How should you treat a calf with scours?
options: B) Give electrolytes and consult vet
quiz.explanation: Electrolytes replace lost fluids, and a vet can advise on further treatment.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records in calf rearing?
options: A) To show off to neighbours
B) To track growth and health
quiz.explanation: Records help you monitor progress, spot problems early, and make informed decisions.

quiz.q: What is the target average daily gain for a healthy calf?
quiz.explanation: A well-fed calf should gain 400-600 grams per day.

quiz.q: What should you do if a calf is not eating?
options: B) Check for sickness and consult vet
quiz.explanation: Loss of appetite is an early sign of illness; quick action is needed.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good biosecurity practice?
options: A) Allow visitors to touch calves
quiz.explanation: Quarantining new animals prevents the spread of diseases to the existing herd.

quiz.q: What is the best way to clean feeding buckets?
options: B) Wash with hot water and soap
D) Leave them in the sun
quiz.explanation: Hot water and soap remove milk residues and kill bacteria.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid feeding milk from a cow treated with antibiotics?
options: B) It can cause antibiotic resistance
D) It makes the calf sleepy
quiz.explanation: Antibiotic residues can lead to resistant bacteria and are harmful to the calf.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a calf jacket?
options: A) To make the calf look pretty
B) To keep the calf warm in cold weather
quiz.explanation: A jacket helps maintain body temperature, especially for young calves in cold conditions.

quiz.q: How often should you disinfect the calf pen?
quiz.explanation: Weekly disinfection reduces pathogen build-up, while daily cleaning removes organic matter.

quiz.q: What is the first step when a calf is born?
options: B) Clear mucus from nose and mouth
quiz.explanation: Clearing the airways ensures the calf can breathe properly.

quiz.q: Which feed is introduced from week 3?
quiz.explanation: Calf starter is a dry feed that helps develop the rumen and should be offered from week 3.

quiz.q: What is the ideal weight of a calf at 6 months?
quiz.explanation: With good feeding, a calf can reach around 200 kg by 6 months.

quiz.q: Why should you not overfeed milk to a calf?
options: B) It makes the calf fat
quiz.explanation: Overfeeding milk can lead to digestive upset and diarrhoea.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to lift a calf?
options: C) With one arm around chest and one around hindquarters
quiz.explanation: Supporting the chest and hindquarters prevents injury to the calf and strain on you.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of good health in a calf?
quiz.explanation: An active, alert calf with bright eyes is a sign of good health.

quiz.q: What should you do with a dead calf?
options: A) Leave it in the pen
B) Bury it deep or incinerate
C) Throw it in the bush
quiz.explanation: Proper disposal prevents the spread of disease to other animals and humans.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a calf is getting enough colostrum?
options: B) It has a full belly and passes meconium
quiz.explanation: A full belly and passing the first dark dung (meconium) indicate the calf has received colostrum.

quiz.q: What is the recommended water temperature for mixing milk replacer?
quiz.explanation: Milk replacer should be mixed with water at about 40Â°C for proper dissolution and digestion.

quiz.q: Why is it important to wean calves gradually?
options: A) To avoid stress and digestive problems
C) To make them grow faster
quiz.explanation: Gradual weaning allows the calf's rumen to adapt to solid feed without setbacks.

quiz.q: What is a good source of starter feed for calves?
quiz.explanation: Commercial calf starter is balanced with energy, protein, and minerals for growing calves.
